newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. tries to repair Moslem-Croat ties.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tries to repair Moslem-Croat ties.

text.p: A senior U.S. envoy said on Wednesday that efforts to merge Bosnian Moslem and Croat armies had suffered a major setback since violence erupted in the southern town of Mostar this month.

James Pardew, who oversees the U.S. military aid programme for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, said meetings and army training sessions had to be cancelled due to tensions between the federation partners.
"We have had a couple of weeks now where this Mostar incident has interfered with progress," Pardew told Reuters.

Meetings between Croat and Moslem defence officials broke down and soldiers failed to show up to military training sessions because Croats were reluctant to drive into Moslem-held territory due to heightened tensions, he said.
"I personnally called on (Federation Defence) Minister (Ante) Jelavic in Mostar to discuss the devastating effect that this had on this programme in the short term," he said.
Pardew said he had made clear to Jelavic, and the top Croat army officer in Bosnia, General Zivko Budimir, that the violence which broke out in Mostar could not be tolerated.
"I told them that the time for nationalist extremists was over, that it's time to name names and remove people who support this kind of activity and to take legal action against criminals."
One Moslem man was shot dead and at least 22 were wounded this month when armed Croat men opened fire and stabbed Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar.
Pardew said Jelavic assured him that the Bosnian Croat military was not involved in the attack.
Jelavic had also spoken to the Moslem deputy defence minister to defuse tensions and "to ensure that this not get out of control", Pardew said.
The U.S.-sponsored "train and equip" programme is supposed to help merge separate Croat and Moslem armies into a single military force which could counter a possible threat from rival Bosnian Serbs.
Croat and Moslem officials are currently discussing a plan to create a single federation defence ministry, which Pardew said was a critical test for the political success of the federation.

Croat officials have requested accommodation in Sarajevo to allow them to work in the capital full-time. But Pardew said Moslem authorities had put the request on hold after a wave of expulsions of Moslem famlies from western Mostar.
"How in the world can I help them get housing in Sarajevo when this kind of thing is happening in Mostar? It just poisons the atmosphere."

International human rights workers say the Bosnian Croat militia has been implicated in "ethnic cleansing" of Moslem families over the past year. Pardew said Washington was monitoring the militia's behaviour closely.
"We're going to watch it very carefully and the time for glossing over this activity is passed...responsible officials are going to be held accountable."

Croat authorities were shown critical U.S. press coverage of the Mostar incident "to make sure they understand the implications of this kind of criminal act on the attitude of the president of the United States toward their particular community."
Pardew said he had discussed the matter with Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak, widely believed to exert heavy influence over the Bosnian Croats. He said Susak had been "helpful".
